keyConcepts: The concept of ''classroom life where classmates build up friendships and exchange information about their daily and study routines
habits and activities in class and at home'' is present in all languages because it is one of the well-known facts that almost all people
go to school and meet different people from different daily and study routines

and activities. Majority of children and young people attend school classes where they build up friendships with their classmates by exchanging information about themselves in terms of their daily and study routines

and activities; students with different daily routines/habits/activities

units.theme: Regular Upper Secondary-Year 9-Level: B1.1 - Theme 3: Personal Lıfe: Physıcal Appearance & Personalıty
fieldSkills: FLFS1. Listening/Watching-Comprehension FLFS2. Reading-Comprehension FLFS3. Speaking-Expression FLFS4. Writing-Expression FLSS1. Grammaring: Selection and Use FLSS2. Vocabulary: Selection and Use FLSS3. Pronunciation: Selection and Use
sel: SELS1.3. Self- Reflection Skill SELS2.1. Communication Skill
interdisciplinary: Atatürk’s Principles and History of Revolution
content: PERSONAL LIFE: PHYSICAL APPEARANCE AND PERSONALITY
Sub-themes: “Physical appearance in terms of physical features and personality in terms of personal traits and characters”
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):
Vocabulary for physical features:
Vocabulary for body weight: Plump, slim, well-built. Vocabulary for body height: Medium-height.

Vocabulary for hair colour/shape: Blond (male), blonde (female), wavy, curly, straight. Vocabulary for skin colour: Brunette, fair (skinned), tan (skinned) pale (skinned), dark (skinned) Vocabulary for age: Middle-aged, elderly.
Vocabulary for physical appearance: Attractive, handsome, good-looking, pretty. Vocabulary for personality:
Adjectives: Smart, clever, confident, cheerful, outgoing, careless, calm, shy, silly, forgetful, honest, brave, serious, gentle, kind, polite, generous, rude, peaceful, quiet, moody.
Vocabulary for describing appearance:
Verbs: To look (like), to sound, to seem.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".

*(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:

-The Present Simple Tense (to be in present) (subject verb agreement with subject pronouns “I, we, you, she, he, they, it): (What does s/he look like? S/he looks very nice.) (What kind of a person is s/he? S/He is a brave person / S/He’s very honest.)
-Too & enough: (S/He’s/is too good. S/He’s/is good enough.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing people’s physical appearances, being in present, describing people’s personalities
-Use of “too & enough”: “Too” indicates degrees (Too means more than necessary. “Enough” indicates the right amount of something)
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
You look amazing!
That sounds great!
She’s/is too young!
What a good person!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
Vowels: i: (/i:/;/ɪ/; /aɪ/)
Consonants: j: (ʒ/); k (/k/), l /l/)
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)
keyConcepts: The concept of ''physical appearance in terms of physical features and personality in terms of personal traits and characters'' is present in all languages because it is a fact that all people have physical appearance and a personality. Majority of people talk about their or others’ physical appearances and personalities to describe themselves and/or others in class
or other places. Engaging in such conversations allows them to describe themselves or others to learn about each other better and build up stronger relationships.

content: FAMILY LIFE
Sub-themes: “Family members’ jobs, work routines, work activities and workplaces”
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):
Vocabulary for jobs:

Nouns: A bank clerk, a security guard, a pharmacist, a photographer, a journalist, an architect, a lawyer, an accountant, a businessperson, a computer programmer, a scientist, a psychologist, a content creator, a virtual assistant, a digital marketer, a counsellor, a client, a patent (holder)
Vocabulary for workplaces:

Nouns: A bank, a shopping centre, a pharmacy, a photography studio, a news agency, an architecture/ architectural firm, a law firm, an accounting firm, a business office, an IT company, a science lab, a clinic, a social media platform, leisure centre, Additional Nouns: brand, brand awareness, Adverbs: remotely.
Vocabulary for action verbs representing family members’ work routines and activities:

Verbs: To serve (customers), to check (IDs), to shoot (photographs), to report (news), to design (buildings), to defend (people), to advise (on finances), to manage (a business), to develop (software), to research, to counsel (people), to publish (online), to organise (organize-AmE) (emails), to promote (products), to retire, to run (a workplace)
Vocabulary for family members: A cousin, a nephew, a niece, stepfather, stepmother, stepson, stepdaughter, relative.

*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations: “29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".

*(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)

*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-The Simple Present Tense: (affirmative, negative, interrogative) (Subject verb agreement with subject pronouns “I, we, you, she, he, they, it”.)
What is her/his job? S/he’s/is a scientist.
What does s/he do? S/he researches a new project. What’s/is your job? I’m/am a photographer.
What do you do? I shoot photographs.
What are your parents’ job? They’re/are architects. What do they do? They design buildings.
-Prepositions of place: at, in, on
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Simple Present Tense: Asking and answering about family members’ and other people’s jobs, describing work activities, identifying workplaces.
-Use of the prepositions of place: Describing where people work.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use: Great job!
S/he made it!
S/he’s/ is in charge of the building.
S/He’s/is responsible for designing the plans.
Target Phonological Sounds in Use: Vowels: o: (/o/, /ɒ/, /ɔ:/) Consonants: m: (/m/), n: (/ŋ/, p: /p/
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

Target Language Grammatical in Use:
-The Simple Present Tense with “or”: (Is this a local or an international festival? This is a local festival in Türkiye.)
-The Simple Present Tense with “Wh- question words”: (What festival is this? It is the Orange Festival.) (What do you cook at the Orange Festival? We cook/make orange jam at the Orange Festival.)

(Where is the Omelette Festival? It is in France. What do they cook? They cook omelette in a very big pan.) (What are the ingredients? The ingredients are eggs, milk, cheese, green peppers and mushrooms.)
(How do they cook it? They put some milk, some eggs, and some mushrooms in a pan, they stir it and cook it.)
-The Present Progressive Tense: (What are you cooking now? We are cooking orange cake now.)
-The Simple Present Tense vs the Present Progressive Tense: (How do they serve it? They serve it with salad and bread but we’re/are serving it with green pepper now.)
Functions of Target Language Grammar in Use:
-Use of “Or”: Asking for options to help someone choose something by using the word “or”.
-Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing habits, routines, regular and repeated actions.
-Use of the Present Progressive Tense: describing actions happening at or around the time of speaking.

-Use of “Wh-questions”: Asking and answering about factual information in the present time with Wh- questions and with the pronouns we/you/they by using the Present Simple Tense and Present Progressive Tense.

-Use of the Simple Present Tense vs the Present Progressive Tense: Comparing the descriptions of general truths, routines and habits by using the Simple Present Tense with actions happening at the present moment and/or around the current time by using the Present Progressive Tense.

fieldSkills: FLFS1. Listening/Watching-Comprehension FLFS2. Reading-Comprehension FLFS3. Speaking-Expression FLFS4. Writing-Expression FLSS1. Grammaring: Selection and Use FLSS2. Vocabulary: Selection and Use FLSS3. Pronunciation: Selection and Use
sel: SELS1.3. SelfReflection Skill SELS2.1. Communication Skill
interdisciplinary: Atatürk’s Principles and History of Revolution
content: LIFE IN THE WORLD & NATURE
Sub-themes:
''Nature, endangered animals, their natural living conditions and habitats, and protection of them"
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):
Vocabulary for endangered animals:
Nouns: A polar bear, a sea turtle, an Asian elephant, a tiger, a whale, a great white shark, a penguin, a panda, a dolphin, a chimpanzee, a cheetah.
Vocabulary for their habitats: Nouns: Grasslands, rainforests, woodlands, jungles, oceans, deserts.
Verbs: To need, to survive, to lessen, to breed, to hunt, to hide, to donate, to save, to protect, to produce, to prevent, to threaten, to reduce, to be at risk, to support, to affect.
Other related vocabulary:
Nouns: A shelter, a disease, a food source, wildlife, volunteer, overhunting, overfishing, sea/marine pollution, air pollution, habitat loss, safety, population, survival, existence.
Adjectives: dedicated, renewable, illegal.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid alFitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)". *(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use: -The Simple Present Tense:
(Which animals are endangered? Leopards, cheetahs, elephants etc. are endangered animals.) (Where do endangered animals live? They live in their habitats.)
(What are their habitats? Their habitats are oceans, deserts, woodlands etc.)
(What are the reasons for their endangerment? Overhunting, water pollution, etc. are the reasons for their endangerment.)
-The Simple Past Tense with Verb “To be”: Was/were; there was/there were (Affirmative, negative, and question forms):

(What was the population of the leopards in the past? There were about 700.000 leopards in the world 50 years ago.) (What is the population of the leopard now? -There are about 250.000 leopards in the world today.) (What was the main habitat of leopards/elephants etc..? Their main habitat was the jungle.)
(Where were the habitats of elephants? Their habitats were woodlands and forests.)
(What were the habitats of endangered animals like 50 years ago? They were cleaner and safer etc. than they are today.)
-Use of “should” as a modal verb: (What should we do to protect endangered animals? We should protect their habitats. We should reduce water/air pollution. We should create safe areas for them.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing facts, situations, and conditions in the past.
-Use of the Simple Past Tense “Verb to be (Was/were)”: Asking and answering for information at a specific time in the past.
-Use of the Simple Past Tense “There was/There were”: Asking and answering about factual information and questioning the existence of things, people, and animals at a specific time in the past.
-Use of the modal “Should”: Describing advice, recommendation (and expectation), describing obligation (and expectation).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
It’s too late! / It’s not too late! Every little bit helps!
Spread the word!
In safe hands!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
Diphthongs: ea: (/eə/), ee: /ɪə/
Consonants: w: (/w/); x: (/ks/)
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)
keyConcepts: The concept of ''endangered animals and their habitats and living conditions including where and how they live today and in the past

and ways to protect them from extinction'' is present in almost all languages. People who start learning a new language bring their pre-existing knowledge with them and transfer it to their new language learning context. For instance
a student of an upper-secondary school in year 9
will know which animals are endangered
and where endangered animals live but will not know how to say these things in another language if this has not yet been covered in their existing curriculum. However
this existing knowledge in their own language will help them recognise
and learn them more easily in a foreign language

content: LIFE IN THE UNIVERSE AND THE FUTURE
Sub-themes: “Films, film genres, futuristic films with futuristic ideas, and technology”
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary): Vocabulary for film genres:

Nouns: Film (movie-AmE), comedy, action, cartoon (animated-AmE), romantic (romance-AmE), family film, adventure, science fiction, detective film, historical film, thriller, mystery, horror, musical, documentary, biographical, crime, martial arts.
Vocabulary for futuristic film genres:

Nouns: Space adventure, robots, alien invasion, time travel, time loop, space exploration, adventure, superheroes, science (sci-fi) fantasy, an invention, a discovery, a survival, an actor, an actress, a director, a crew, virtual reality, a myth. Verbs: To discover, to explore, to invent, to adapt, to control, to be into sth. Adjectives: Futuristic, robotic, artificial, virtual, technological, horrific, world-saving, legendary, global, optimistic, intelligent, epic.

*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations: “29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".

*(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Background Grammatical Structures in Use:
-The Simple Present Tense: (Adventure films show exciting places and happening.)

*About “Background Grammatical Structures in Use”: The “Background Grammatical Structures” in this section are not only revisional but also serve as contextual support and contribute to meaning-making. They are intended to be used within the theme to help students grasp the meaning of the language constructed through the use of “Target Grammatical Structures” without being explicitly taught. These structures are not considered “Target Grammatical Structures” themselves rather they function as a part of the facilitation process, supporting both the target forms and the contexts in which they are used. They provide opportunities for learning through revised and scaffolded language.

Target Grammatical Structures in Use: -The Simple Future Tense (Positive, negative, Interrogative): (What (do you think) will happen in the future? (I think) robots will help people in the future. People will travel to other planets. Scientists will invent new machines to explore space. Time travellers will change history. People will live in virtual reality worlds.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing events and happenings (in films).

-Use of the Simple Future Tense: Describing predictions, expressing what speakers believe and expect, explaining speakers’ opinions or guesses about the future, describing advice, recommendations (and expectations).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
This (film) is a breath of fresh air!
This (film) is not my cup of tea!
I’m not brave enough to watch this!
What’s next?
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
Diphthong: o, oe, owoa, ou, eau: /əʊ/
Consonants: y: (/j/, /i/; z: (/z/)
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

content: SCHOOL LIFE & EDUCATION
Sub-themes: "Comparing different school systems (local and international) and different education systems; school traditions, events, and celebration activities; national days and celebrations''
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):
Vocabulary for comparing different school systems (local and international):
Nouns: A schedule, a process, a curriculum, a structure, an evaluation, diversity, a scheme, a separation.
Verbs: To differ, to eliminate, to adapt, to vary, to distinguish.
Adjectives: Compulsory, distinct, diverse, comprehensive, flexible, structural, intense, broad, efficient, distinct, unequal, comparable.

Adverbs: Adequately, appropriately, consequently, considerably, critically, efficiently, extensively, primarily. Phrases for different education systems: Individual learning, critical thinking, an extracurricular activity, global citizenship, a multilingual education.
Vocabulary for comparing different education and school systems: Prepositions: Unlike. Conjunctions: whereas, while. Adverb: Yet.
Prepositional phrases: in comparison, compared to, contrary to.
Adverbial Phrases: on the contrary, in contrast, on the other hand.
Vocabulary for school traditions, events and celebrations:

Nouns: A school badge, a competition, an award, a tradition, a parade, a debate, a contestant, opening day activities (icebreakers, orientation sessions), an educational excursion, a dance recital, a raffle, an award ceremony.
Verbs: to compete, to perform, to participate, to gather, to present, to volunteer, to host, to support, to cheer.
Adjectives: Annual, traditional, collaborative.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, “Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)”, “Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)”. *(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:

-The Simple Present Tense with certain Verbs: (like, prefer, understand, want, need, know, mean, believe, remember, forget) vs the Present Progressive Tense: (The school wants to organize a book fair. Yet, the students are joining a sports tournament now).
- Adverbs of Frequency (always, never, seldom, sometimes, often, etc): (The curriculum always differs from school to school).
- ''May and Might'' for Polite Requests: (May I see your passport?)
- ''Can and Could'' for Polite Requests: (Can I see the manager? Could you say it again?)
- Articles and Quantifiers (A, an, the, zero article, one): (This international school hosts a folk dance recital every year)
-Question Tags with the Simple Present Tense and the Present Progressive Tense: (She is organising an art exhibition, isn’t she?)
- ''Shall'' for Polite Requests: (Shall we go to the exhibition?)
Functions of the Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Simple Present Tense vs the Present Progressive Tense: Contrasting what usually happens with what is happening now.
-Different uses of the Simple Present Tense: (Newspaper Headlines: Schools close on Thursday). (Emphatic Use: I do like my school) (Imperative Use: Every Monday, you stand in line for the assembly).

-Use of Adverbs of Frequency: Expressing how often certain activities or routines take place in schools; describing patterns in students’ participation or stress-related issues. -Use of ''May, Might, Can, Could'' for Polite Questions: Asking polite questions.
-Use of Articles and Quantifiers (A, an, the, zero article, one): Introducing nouns and providing information about the specificity and countability of nouns.
-Use of Question Tags with the Simple Present Tense and the Present Progressive Tense: Confirming or clarifying information.
-Use of ''Shall'' for Polite Requests: Offering or proposing politely.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
Education is the passport to the future.
Teamwork makes the dream work!
Stay curious, stay hungry for knowledge!
We have different systems, but the goal is the same.
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
-Intonation for positive statements, negative statements, questions, and question tags.
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme).

content: CLASSROOM LIFE & LEARNING
Sub-themes: "Favourite school subjects, learning activities, study tools and innovations''
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):

Vocabulary for favourite school subjects and learning activities: Nouns: Passion, curiosity, satisfaction, confidence, inspiration, success, motivation. Verbs: To activate, to appreciate, to look forward to, to discover, to succeed in, to grasp. Adjectives: Engaging, inspiring, rewarding, satisfying, passionate, practical, educational, productive. Nouns: Frustration, boredom, confusion, tension, anxiety, struggle, failure, reluctance, avoidance, exhaustion, demotivation.
Verbs: To avoid, to ignore, to complain, to tolerate, to skip, to lose interest, to give up.
Adjectives: Confusing, frustrating, exhausting, irrelevant.
Vocabulary for favourite learning activities:

Nouns: A debate, a presentation, a group discussion, a brainstorming session, art and craft, a quiz competition, storytelling, creating a model, field research, memorization, a repetition practice, doing a drill, silent reading, note-taking.
Vocabulary for favourite study tools and innovations:
Adjectives: Efficient, user-friendly, accessible, out of date, complicated, inconvenient, old-fashioned.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, “Eid al Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)”, “Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)”.

*(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-The Simple Present Tense for the Future: (The presentation starts in ten minutes).
-The Present Progressive Tense for the Future: (I am writing an essay tonight).
-The Present Progressive Tense with Always: (He is always postponing his duties).
-Question Tags for Related Tenses: (He is always complaining about field research, isn’t he?)
-Making Adverbs from Adjectives (Regular and Irregular): They are quick runners. They run quickly).
-Adjectives with -ed vs -ing: (Group discussions are complicated).
-Correlative Conjunctions (either, neither): (She isn’t attending a group discussion next week, either).
-Elliptical Responses (So do I, I hope so, etc.): (She likes brainstorming sessions. So do I).
Functions of the Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Simple Present Tense for the Future: Describing scheduled future events fixed with timetables or plans.
-Use of the Present Progressive Tense for the Future: Describing planned future actions that are already arranged or decided.
-Use of the Present Progressive Tense with always: Describing actions that cause irritation.
-Use of Adverbs Made from Adjectives: Describing where, how, when, to what extent some things happen.
-Use of Question Tags for Related Tenses: Confirming or clarifying information.
-Use of Adjectives with -ed vs -ing: Describing the thing or situation that causes the feeling.
-Use of Correlative Conjunctions (either, neither): Describing two alternatives or a negative choice between two alternatives.
-Use of Elliptical Responses (So do I, I hope so, etc.): Giving brief answers in a conversation to avoid unnecessary repetition.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
Mistakes are proof you’re trying!
Ask questions, grow smarter!
This class is our learning playground!
I meant to do it, but I totally spaced out.

units.theme: Upper Secondary-Year 9 (After Prep)-Level: B2.1 - Theme 3: Personal Lıfe & Well-Beıng
content: PERSONAL LIFE & WELL-BEING
Sub-themes: "Physical health (body and illnesses); personal well-being with mental and emotional health; personal well-being with social health''
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):
Vocabulary for personal well-being with physical health (body and illnesses):

Nouns: A lung, a joint, a heel, a consultant, healthcare, herb, hunger, a pill, recovery, a surgeon, survival, a first-aid kit, a bacterium, a cell, a mineral, relief, a surgery, a vitamin, a fever, a stroke, a cancer, a wound, an injury, anxiety, depression, an addiction, a recovery, a disability, panic, medication, an infection, a symptom, a treatment.
Verbs: To breathe, to consult, to heal, to cure, to suffer, to swallow, to operate, to bother.
Adjectives: Balanced, adequate, disabled, relieved, short-term, urgent, conscious, longterm, severe, unconscious.
Adverbs: Terribly, accidentally, adequately, appropriately, instantly, severely, strictly.

Vocabulary for personal well-being with mental and emotional health: Nouns: Mental health, psychological health, social bond/involvement, family tie, confidence, fulfilment, balance, self-awareness, empathy.
Vocabulary for practices and actions with mental and emotional health: Nouns: Mindfulness, therapy, breathing exercises, relaxation, rehabilitation.
Vocabulary for personal well-being with social health: Nouns: Loneliness, isolation, alienation, social anxiety, conflict, relief, pride, confusion, disappointment, trust, adaptation, acceptance.
Verbs: To interact, to socialise, to participate, to maintain, to contribute, to volunteer, to strengthen, to support.
Vocabulary for social relationship: Nouns: An acquaintance, a colleague, a community member, a mentor.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, “Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)”, “Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)”.

*(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-The Simple Past Tense versus the Past Progressive Tense: (She was suffering from a headache when her friend called her yesterday).
-Could for Ability: (I could exercise for 30 minutes without interruption when I was younger).
-Used to: (He used to socialise for his well-being).
-Would: (When I was a kid, we would visit my grandparents every summer holiday).
-Wh- questions (How long, etc.): (How long did your friend suffer from depression?).
-Question Tags with Related Tenses: (She healed after the surgery, didn’t she?)
-Prepositions: (among, until, on, at, in, in case, by, of, with, about, to, for, from, out of): (The consultant helped him cope with his depression).
-Prepositional Phrases with in, for, to, at, about, with, from, of, etc.: (She struggled with frustration after the teacher announced the exam results).

-Either, Neither, So do I, I hope so: (She can either take a short walk or do some breathing exercises to feel better). (Neither stress nor overthinking is good for your mental wellbeing). (I believe taking time for ourselves is important. So do I).(Doctors say regular exercise improves our health. I hope so!).
Functions of the Grammatical Structures in Use:

-Use of the Simple Past Tense versus the Past Progressive Tense: Describing an action that was interrupted by another event (The Past Progressive Tense) or completed in the past (The Simple Past Tense).

-Use of ''Could'' (for Ability): Describing an ability in the past. -Use of ''Used to''): Describing past habits or routines that do not occur in the present. -Use of ''Would'' for past habits: Describing things which happen in the past as habit or repeated action but no longer happens.
-Use of ''Wh- questions'' (How long, etc.): Asking for specific information about a subject, an object, time, a place, manner and a reason.
-Use of Question Tags with Related Tenses: Asking short questions to confirm or clarify information in the sentence.

-Use of Prepositions: (among, until, on, at, in, in case, by, of, with, about, to, for, from, out of): Indicating relationship among the components of a sentence in terms of cause, direction, manner, time, and location.
-Use of Prepositional Phrases with in, for, from, to, at, about, with, from, of, etc.: Clarifying the details in the sentence about the cause, direction, manner, time, and location.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
Healthy mind, healthy life!
Self-care isn’t selfish!
You’re stronger than you think!
I just need a break today!
Let’s chill for a bit!

-Intonation for positive statements, negative statements, questions, and question tags.

units.theme: Upper Secondary-Year 9 (After Prep)-Level: B2.1 - Theme 4: Famıly Lıfe & Home
content: FAMILY LIFE & HOME
Sub-themes: "Housing diversity in the world; intergenerational issues and family problems on daily conflicts and sharing the same house; relationships between the family and the community''
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):
Vocabulary for housing diversity in the world:

Nouns: An apartment (a flat Amer.), a single-family house, a bungalow, a duplex/triplex house, a two-storey house, a skyscraper, a slum, a hut, a basement, a cellar, a chimney, an attic, a shutter, a fence, a terrace.
Adjectives: Awkward, unique, affordable, luxurious, contemporary, charming, elegant.
Vocabulary for intergenerational issues and family problems on daily conflicts and sharing the same house:
Nouns: A disagreement, a tension, a misunderstanding, a dispute, criticism, blame, an interruption, neglect, exclusion.
Verbs: To quarrel, to negotiate, to interrupt, to adjust.

Phrases for intergenerational issues and family problems on sharing the same house: A generation gap, traditional and modern belief, family value, a shared interest, a parent-child conflict, elderly care, a family dynamic, a communication barrier, an emotional distance, a parental pressure, a shared responsibility, a noise conflict, a lack of personal space.
Vocabulary for relationships between the family and the community: Nouns: An ancestor, an apology, a bond, a connection, participation, cooperation.
Verbs: To connect, to contribute, to volunteer, to promote, to assist, to welcome.
Phrasal Verbs for relationships: To fall out (with someone), get on well (with someone).
Adverbs: Altogether.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, “Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)”, “Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)”. *(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:

-The Present Perfect Tense vs the Present Perfect Progressive Tense (for, since, yet, already, never, ever, just, recently): (My family have just moved to a two-storey house in the country. Have you ever volunteered to do a household chore? We have been living in a detached house since the 2020 earthquake).
-Comparative and Superlative of Irregular Adjectives (e.g. far - further/farther - furthest/farthest: (Our ancestors had to walk further to school than we do now).
-Reflexive Pronouns: myself, himself, herself, himself, ourselves, yourself, themselves: (We have always encouraged each other to express ourselves openly in our family discussions.)
-Wh- questions e.g. How long, etc.: (How long has your father shared his responsibilities with you?).
Functions of the Grammatical Structures in Use:

-Use of the Present Perfect Tense (for, since, yet, already, never, ever, just, recently) vs the Present Perfect Progressive Tense: Discriminating between ongoing activities that began in the past and are still happening now and activities that recently stopped but have clear effects or evidence in the present.
-Use of Comparative and Superlative of Irregular Adjectives (i.e. far - further / farther - furthest / farthest): Describing and comparing people, objects, and/or situations.

-Use of Reflexive Pronouns (myself, himself, herself, himself, ourselves, yourself, themselves): Saying the subject performs an action on itself or emphasising that the subject performed the action independently or without help.
-Use of Wh- questions i.e. How long, etc.: Asking about the duration of an action or event).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
Family is life’s greatest blessing!
Love, laugh, and listen!
This is our family motto!
My little brother is really getting on my nerves!
We argue, but we still care about each other as a family!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
Vowels: a, e
Consonants: b, c, d
Vowels: a: (/ae/, /aeı/, /ə/, /a:/, /eɪ/, /a:/, /a/, /ɔː/, /eə/); e: (/e/; /i:/, /ə/, silent /e/)
Consonant: b: (/b/), silent /b/); c: (/si/, /k/, /tʃ/, /z/, silent /c/); d: (/d/), silent /d/)
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme).

units.theme: Upper Secondary-Year 9 (After Prep)-Level: B2.1 - Theme 5: Lıfe In The Neıghbourhood, Cıty & Socıal Lıfe
content: LIFE IN THE NEIGHBOURHOOD, CITY & SOCIAL LIFE
Sub-themes: "City development and infrastructure; urban and rural lifestyles; future of cities''
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):

Vocabulary for city development and infrastructure: Nouns: An analyst, a budget, a cable, a committee, concrete, a construction, a council, an estate, an institution, immigration, a lane, a mayor, a zone. Verbs: To accommodate, to anticipate, to calculate, to construct, to distribute, to govern, to propose, to disturb, to rebuild, to transform, to lay (pipes, cables), to renovate, to restore, to strengthen. Adjectives: Lively, urban, efficient, developed, vibrant.

Vocabulary for urban and rural lifestyles: Nouns: An arrow, a cliff, a shelter, a brick, a district. Verbs: To abandon, to dig, to wander. Adjectives for urban lifestyles: Diverse, fastpaced, commercial, energetic, charming, dynamic, entertaining, outstanding. Adjectives for rural lifestyles: Tranquil, peaceful, slow-paced, remote, authentic, tropical, unique, conventional, distant. Adverbs: Aside.
Vocabulary for Future Cities: Adjectives: Advanced, sustainable, innovative, high-tech, eco-friendly, flexible, accessible, energy-efficient, global. Adverbs: Automatically.
Vocabulary for challenges to overcome in future of cities: Nouns: Privacy, overpopulation, resource management. Phrasal verbs: Put aside.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, “Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)”, “Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)”. *(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-The Simple Future Tense vs Be Going to Future Tense: (The committee will restore the museum. The officials are going to rebuild this zone for security).

-Connecting Words Expressing Cause and Effect, Contrast: (so, which, until, why, while, when, as, before, after, as long as, whenever, whereas, but, by the time, even though, despite, etc.): (The city is crowded and fast-paced, in contrast, rural areas are calm and spacious).
Functions of the Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Simple Future Tense versus Be Going to Future Tense: Discriminating future plans, predictions, planned actions from unplanned actions and spontaneous decisions.

-Use of Connecting Words Expressing Cause and Effect, Contrast: (so, which, until, why, while, when, as, before, after, as long as, whenever, whereas, but, by the time, even though, despite, in spite of, etc.): Clarifying the relationship between the ideas about life in the neighbourhood and social life.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
Let’s meet up at the new café!
It’s quicker if we take the tram.
There’s a cool spot near the square!
This city never sleeps!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
Vowels: i: (/aı/, /ı/, /i:/)
Consonants: f: (/f/); g: (/g/, /dʒ/, silent /g/); h: (/h/), silent /h/); j: (/dʒeɪ/, /dʒ/); k: (/k/, silent /k/)
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme).
keyConcepts: The target concept of this theme ''life in the neighbourhood

city and social life with its components such as city development and infrastructure; urban and rural lifestyles; future of cities'' is present in almost all languages. Students who start to learn a new language inevitably bring with them their pre-existing knowledge and transfer it to their new language learning context. For example
a student (year 9-after prep) of an upper secondary school may know what ''life in the neighbourhood
city and social life with its components such as city development and infrastructure; urban and rural lifestyles; future of cities'' means
but may not know how to say these things in a foreign language if this has not yet been covered in their existing curriculum. However
this existing knowledge in their own language will help them recognise
and learn the new information more easily in a foreign language

units.theme: Upper Secondary-Year 9 (After Prep)-Level: B2.1 - Theme 6: Lıfe In The World & Culture
content: LIFE IN THE WORLD & CULTURE
Sub-themes: "Global cuisines, food habits and cultures; cultural diversity and international sports, films and musical events; impact of globalisation on everyday life''

Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary): Vocabulary for global cuisines, food habits and cultures: Nouns: Consumption, a combination, flavour, nutrition, obesity, a portion, a preference, protein, spice. Verbs: To chop, to manufacture, to swallow.
Adjectives: Affordable, balanced, beneficial, dairy, organic.
Vocabulary for cultural diversity and international sports events: Nouns: Conservation, a leaflet, a legend, a myth, a parade. Verbs: To adapt, to classify, to distinguish, to inherit.

Adjectives: Appropriate, mixed, precious. Adverbs: Genuinely. International sports events: Nouns: An applicant, a marathon, a medal, a membership, a referee, a spectator, a sponsorship, an opponent, a representative, a pitch, a venue.
Verbs: To broadcast, to cheer, to equip. Adjectives: Entertaining, risky, skilled. Adverbs: Severely.
Impact of globalisation on everyday life: Nouns: A civilization, fame. Verbs: To dominate, to edit, to exploit.
Adjectives: industrial, universal, widespread. Adverbs: Apparently, extensively, rapidly.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, “Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)”, “Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)”. *(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Modals for Probability: (''Can, Could, May, Might, Must''): (The combination of organic vegetables can provide a better source of nutrition).
-Modals for Lack of Probability (''Can’t, Couldn’t''): (That can’t be dessert. It’s too sour!)
-Modals for Speculation: (''Can, Could, May, Might, Must, Can’t, Couldn’t''): (She must be the assistant chef of this restaurant).
-Modals for Deduction (''Must, Can’t, Might, May, Could''): (The meal must be high in protein because it’s made of meat).
-Modals for Obligation and Necessity (''Must, Have to, Need'') Obligation in the Past (''Had to''): (They must wash their hands before cooking the food).
-Modals for lack of Obligation (''Don’t have to- Don’t need to, Needn’t''): (You don’t have to eat that soup if it doesn’t taste good).

-Modals for Prohibition (''Must not - Can’t''): (You can’t enter the kitchen. You don’t work here). -Modals for Lack of Prohibition (Modals for Permission) (''Can, may, could''): (You could learn the recipe if you like).
-Modals for Advice (''Should, Ought to, Had better, Could''): (You should try Turkish ''Dolma'' if you want to taste traditional food in Türkiye)
-Be Able to in the Present and Future: (People will be able to reach global markets more easily due to developments in technology in the future).
Functions of the Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of Modals (''Can, Could, May, Might, Must''): Expressing probability and speculation.
-Use of Modals (''Can’t, Couldn’t''): Expressing lack of Probability. -Use of Modals (''Could, Must, Can’t, Might, May''): Expressing deduction.
-Use of Modals (''Must, Have to, Need'') Obligation in the Past (''Had to''): Expressing obligation and necessity.
-Use of Modals (''Don’t have to, Don’t need to, Needn’t''): Expressing lack of obligation.
-Use of Modals (''Must not - Can’t''): Expressing prohibition. -Use of Modals (Modals for Permission) (''Can, may, could''): Expressing lack of prohibition.
-Modals for Advice (''Should, Ought to, Had better, Could''): Expressing advice and recommendation.
-Use of ''Be Able to in the Present and Future'' (''Am-is-are able to, will be able to'': Expressing ability.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
That’s part of our tradition!
Let me show you something from our culture!
Different is interesting, not weird!
Culture brings us closer!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
Vowel: o
Consonants: l, m, n, (ng), p
Vowel: o: (/əʊ/, /ɒ/, /əʊ/)
Consonants: l: (/ɛl/ /l/, silent /l/); m; (/ɛm/,/m/); n: (/ɛn/, /n/, silent /n/); ng: (/ng/); p: (piː//p/, silent /p/)

units.theme: Upper Secondary-Year 9 (After Prep)-Level: B2.1 - Theme 8: Lıfe In The Unıverse & The Future
content: LIFE IN THE UNIVERSE & THE FUTURE
Sub-themes: "Universal issues in the future; search for habitable planets; space and technology''
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary):

Vocabulary for life in the universe: Nouns: Globe, oxygen, carbon, observation. Verbs: To observe. Adjectives: Mysterious, solar, essential, external, outer, unknown. Adverbs: Essentially, universally.

Vocabulary for habitable planets: Nouns: Existence, an exploration, an inhabitant, an astronomer, a civilisation, a mission, a satellite, a rocket, a colony, radiation. Verbs: To attempt, to estimate, to detect, to launch, to settle. Adjectives: Distant, dynamic, massive, potential. Adverbs: Beyond, potentially, elsewhere. Vocabulary for space and technology: Nouns: An alien, a database, an aircraft, privacy, navigation. Verbs: To implement, to interact, to install, to advance, to transform.
Adjectives: Sophisticated, efficient, curious, artificial.
Phrases: Space mission, interplanetary travel
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations:

“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, “Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)”, “Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)”. *(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme

In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Zero Conditional: (If you heat water to 100 degrees Celsius, it boils).
-Conditional 1: (If we leave early in the morning, we will have enough time to explore the city centre).
-Conditional 2: (If we found another planet to live on, would people travel there?).
-Wish Clauses: (I wish our planet could be a better place to live).
Functions of the Grammatical Structures in Use:
-Use of the Zero Conditional: Describing general truths, facts, and habits-situations where the result always happens if the condition is met.
-Use of the Conditional 1: Describing realistic situations in future that are likely to happen and/or cause-andeffect relationship between a condition and its probable outcome.
-Use of the Conditional 2: Describing imaginary, unlikely, and unreal situations in the present or future and their results.
-Use of ''Wish Clauses'': Describing regrets, desires, and/or unreal situations about the present, future and the past.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use:
What do you think the future will be like?
Would you go to space if you could?
Sounds like sci-fi - but maybe not.
The future is closer than we think!
Big ideas start with small questions!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use:
Consonants: v, w, x, y, z
Consonants: v: (/viː/, /v/); w: (/w/), silent /w/); x: (/ɛks/, /ks/, /gz/); y: (/waɪ/, /j/, /ɪ/, /iː/); z: /(zed/ (Br), /ziː/ (AmE), /z/)
*(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme).
keyConcepts: The target concept of this theme ''life in the universe and the future with its components such as universal issues in the future; search for habitable planets; space and technology'' is present in almost all languages. Students who start to learn a new language inevitably bring with them their pre-existing knowledge and transfer it to their new language learning context. For example

a student (year 9-after prep) of an upper secondary school may know what ''life in the universe and the future with its components such as universal issues in the future; search for habitable planets; space and technology'' means
but may not know how to say these things in a foreign language if this has not yet been covered in their existing curriculum. However
this existing knowledge in their own language will help them recognise
and learn the new information more easily in a foreign language
